To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a conditioned fear stimulus attenuates freezing in response to footshock in rats, and that naloxone blocks this attenuation.
a CS that signals shock attenuates shock-induced freezing, with this attenuation occurring several minutes later and lasting for several days, and that the effect is reversible by naloxone.
fear conditioning can increase pain responsiveness, and that naloxone can block this effect.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of conditioned fear in the regulation of pain responsiveness.
the effects of fear on pain responsiveness and with the mechanisms that mediate these effects.
how fear and pain interact to influence responsiveness to pain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the conditioned fear stimulus attenuated freezing to shock, and the attenuation occurred several minutes after the presentation of shock; this effect was blocked by naloxone and it was retained over an extended interval.
fear can induce hyperalgesia and analgesia in different experimental situations, and that naloxone can reverse the effects of conditioned fear on pain responsiveness.
the fear CS attenuates freezing in response to a shock, and that naloxone blocks this effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fear stimulus has a long-term effect on the pain responsiveness of the organism, which is reversible by an opioid antagonist.
fear conditioning produces a state of generalized hyperalgesia, which is reversed by naloxone.
the effects of a conditioned fear CS on pain responsiveness depend on the type of pain measure used and on the time after conditioning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of conditioned fear on nociception are not simple.
the fear CS can produce analgesia and that this effect can be retained for long periods of time and can be blocked by the opioid antagonist naloxone.
fear learning can have long-term and enduring effects, and that fear learning may affect nociception in a manner that differs from its effects on freezing.
